newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Rafale fighter in danger from budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: France's Rafale fighter in danger from budget cuts.

text.p: Production of France's Rafale fighter-bomber has been halted since April and the entire programme is under threat from budget cutbacks, a parliamentary report on France's air force budget said on Tuesday.

"The Rafale programme is today in a state of peril, not for technical reasons, for its success appears in all cases as exceptional, but for budgetary reasons," assemblyman Olivier Darrason said in the report.
The report noted that the new defence budget which covers spending from 1997 to 2001, puts off until 2005 from an original date of mid-2002, the creation of the first Rafale squadron of 20 jets.
Over the five-year period covered by the budget, the government expects to order 48 Rafales, 15 for the navy and 33 configured for the air force. Only 14 will be delivered during that period.
The plane's producers have offered a 10 percent cut in the price of the planes in exchange for a firm, multi-year order for the entire 1997-2002 production.
Such a commitment would take away the uncertainty of typical government orders, which can be called into question from one year to the next, industrialists said.

Cuts in the defence budget have forced Dassault to examine novel methods of financing the Rafale programme. One solution being studied is for the firms in the programme to fund 10 planes and lease them to the air force, defence industry sources have said.

To aid the export of the plane, Darrason said he was in favour of an "extrabudgetary" solution to financing the plane. This would allow the programme to deliver some 10 planes for service by 2002, as Dassault wants.

Darrason said a bank loan of three or four billion francs could be taken out to fund about 10 planes, but it is unclear who would pay the interest on the loan, expected to come to 600 to 700 million francs.
"Right now, this matter is not moving forward because of the uncertainty over payment of financing costs," Darrason said.

"Both the firms and the ministry of defence want the order, but neither want to bear the cost," he said, adding that it was "unimaginable that the government would not carry some of the financing burden."
